findings.consequence: A caller/observer sees a different exception type than the one that actually caused the failure (violating Design Decision D5's stated intent to 're-raise the original exception unchanged'), loses the diagnostic log line documenting the release attempt, and — in the worst case — the event is left claimed forever with no observability into why, silently converting a transient release failure into the same unrecoverable-stuck-payment state the plan already accepts as an out-of-scope limitation, but now via an unlogged path.
findings.failure_scenario: fulfil(event.payment_id) raises (e.g. RuntimeError), entering the except block; before the bare `raise` executes, self._repository.release_for_retry(event.provider_event_id) itself raises (e.g. sqlite3.OperationalError if the on-disk store is locked beyond the 30s busy-timeout, or any other I/O error). The new exception propagates instead of the original fulfilment exception, the 'claim released for retry' log line never runs, and — depending on whether release_for_retry's DELETE committed before failing — the claim row may remain in place, permanently blocking any future retry for that provider_event_id with no evidence in the logs that release was attempted or failed.
findings.reason: This is an untested corner case in the exception-handling/transaction-recovery path (concurrency/transaction semantics is a protected category per pr-review.md), and fixing it requires an interpretive decision (how should a release failure be surfaced/logged, and should the original exception be preserved via chaining or something stronger) rather than a mechanical, deterministically-verifiable local patch — no existing test pins down the desired behavior for this branch.
findings.remediation_direction: Wrap the release_for_retry() call in its own try/except inside the failure branch (or otherwise guarantee the original exception is what propagates and that release-failure is itself logged), and add a targeted test that makes release_for_retry() fail during the except-block handling to pin down the intended behavior.

findings.consequence: Operationally, a genuine fulfilment failure that triggered a claim release could be missed by monitoring that filters on WARNING/ERROR, delaying detection of a stuck-payment scenario the plan already flags as a known limitation requiring visibility.
findings.failure_scenario: A real fulfilment failure (e.g. a downstream error worth paging on) is logged at INFO level with the same severity as routine duplicate-callback notices, making it indistinguishable from benign traffic in any log-level-based alerting or filtering that treats INFO as non-actionable.
findings.location: process_callback(), except Exception block, logger.info call for the fulfilment-failure message
findings.reason: This is a one-line, local logging-level change with no behavioral or API impact, no interaction with protected categories, and existing tests (which only assert on the 'duplicate' substring at INFO on a different code path) would still pass after the change, so correctness can be established deterministically.
findings.remediation_direction: Log the fulfilment-failure branch at WARNING or ERROR level (e.g. logger.warning or logger.exception) instead of INFO, while keeping the duplicate-callback message at INFO.

summary: The diff closely implements the approved plan's T1/T2/T4/T5 tasks: fulfilment is now gated on record_if_new()'s claim result, a release_for_retry() delete-then-reinsert mechanism restores FR-2 retry capability, the duplicate-vs-first log distinction satisfies AC-3, the controller is correctly left unchanged (AC-2/FR-4), and WAL/busy-timeout hardening plus a barrier-synchronized two-thread test exercise genuine persistence-layer contention for FR-3/C-5. Verification evidence (compileall + full unittest discovery) passed. Two narrow, non-blocking issues were found: an untested edge case where a failure inside release_for_retry() itself would mask the original fulfilment exception and skip the release log, and a minor log-severity choice for the fulfilment-failure path. Neither contradicts the approved plan or its acceptance criteria.
